articles.title: A California reservoir forecasting system could add enough usable water to save $100 million to $200 million a year without building a new reservoir, a study estimates
articles.summary: Science News: California’s water problem is often framed around the need for more storage, new infrastructure and expensive construction. But a new study suggests t.
articles.body: California’s water problem is often framed around the need for more storage, new infrastructure and expensive construction. But a new study suggests that part of the answer may already be sitting behind the state’s existing dams. By using better weather and water forecasts to decide when reservoirs should release or retain water, California could potentially make substantially more water available each year without constructing another reservoir. The research, published in Environmental Research: Water, estimates that Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO) could increase water availability by about 315,000 acre-feet annually, equivalent to more than 100 billion gallons. The researchers estimate that the additional agricultural and urban water supply could generate about $145 million a year in direct economic benefits, with the broader estimated range reaching roughly $100 million to $200 million annually. The primary study was led by researchers from Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego and other institutions.Making existing reservoirs work harderThe basic idea behind FIRO is relatively straightforward. Reservoir operators traditionally have to balance two competing needs: keeping enough empty space to protect downstream communities from floods while retaining enough water to meet future demand. That can be difficult in California because much of the state's water arrives during a relatively small number of powerful winter storms. Atmospheric rivers can deliver huge amounts of precipitation within a short period, rapidly changing conditions from drought concerns to flood threats.FIRO attempts to give reservoir operators better information before making those decisions. Instead of relying primarily on fixed operating rules or calendar-based schedules, operators can use improved forecasts of atmospheric rivers, rainfall and reservoir inflows. If forecasts indicate that a major storm is approaching, water can potentially be released beforehand to create additional storage space. On the other hand, when forecasts indicate that significant inflows are unlikely, operators may be able to retain more water instead of releasing it simply because traditional rules require additional flood-control space. The objective is therefore not simply to store more water. It is to make storage decisions more responsive to what the weather and watershed are actually expected to do.20 reservoirs examinedThe study examined 20 major California reservoirs identified as having no prohibitive barriers to further FIRO assessment. Together, they represent more than 20 million acre-feet of storage capacity, roughly half of California's surface-water storage capacity. Using historical reservoir storage records, researchers estimated how much additional water could potentially have been retained if forecast-informed operations had been available. Their central estimate was approximately 315,000 acre-feet of additional water per year. In particularly wet years, the potential could rise to nearly 500,000 acre-feet, or about 162 billion gallons, enough for more than a million households, according to the researchers. The economic value also varies depending on water conditions. The primary study estimates approximately $145 million per year in direct benefits on average. Its modelling found estimated annual benefits of about $206 million in moderately wet years, compared with roughly $100 million in dry years and $134 million in wet years.More than a water-supply benefitThe researchers stress that the economic estimate is conservative because it focuses mainly on direct benefits to agricultural and urban water users. Other potential benefits were not fully included in that calculation. These could include improved flood-risk management, environmental flows, hydropower generation, fisheries and recreation. Evidence already shows that forecast-informed operations can produce significant results. At a FIRO project, officials said the approach had allowed enough water to be safely retained to supply approximately 250,000 homes for a year, with an estimated economic value of around $125 million.Not a replacement for new projectsThe findings do not suggest that California can solve its water challenges simply by changing reservoir operations. The researchers examined a more ambitious scenario in which forecast-informed operations increased water availability by 5% of gross reservoir capacity. That could produce approximately 1 million acre-feet of additional water and nearly $460 million in direct agricultural and urban benefits, but achieving that level would depend on individual reservoir conditions, improved forecasts, operational changes and potentially targeted infrastructure improvements.According to the researchers, detailed assessments of individual reservoirs are needed before wider implementation. Those assessments would need to consider operational constraints, costs, environmental effects and the full range of benefits. FIRO is ultimately presented as one tool within a much larger water strategy. Conservation, groundwater recharge and new infrastructure would still have roles to play. But the study suggests that California may be able to obtain considerably more value from reservoirs it has already built simply by combining them with better forecasting and more flexible decision-making.

articles.title: In 2018, scientists began removing about 285,000 fish from Wisconsin's McDermott Lake; 4 years later yellow perch were up 788%, but walleye recruitment was still zero
articles.summary: Science News: Scientists removed about 285,000 warm-water fish from a Wisconsin lake over four years in an attempt to help its declining walleye population recover..
articles.body: Scientists removed about 285,000 warm-water fish from a Wisconsin lake over four years in an attempt to help its declining walleye population recover. The large-scale experiment reduced several fish species and was followed by a sharp rise in yellow perch. However, it did not restore natural walleye recruitment.According to Wiley online library, the experiment was carried out at McDermott Lake in Iron County, northern Wisconsin, between 2018 and 2021. The lake covers about 33 hectares. Around 285,100 fish, weighing about 3,190 kg in total were removed from the lake. The fish belonged to a group called centrarchids, which includes species such as bluegill, black crappie, largemouth bass, pumpkinseed and rock bass.Scientists were testing whether removing these fish could reduce competition and predation faced by young walleye. Walleye are an important game fish in north-central North America and support recreational and tribal fisheries. According to the study published in Fisheries Management and Ecology, walleye abundance in Wisconsin had fallen by about 36% over the previous two decades, with failures in natural recruitment identified as a key problem.The results, however, showed that reducing centrarchids alone was not enough to bring back naturally produced young walleye. No age-0 walleye were collected during the study, meaning there was no detectable natural restoration in either McDermott Lake or the reference Sandy Beach Lake.The fish removal experimentThe experiment focused on the idea that growing numbers of warm-water fish could be affecting walleye. Centrarchid numbers had increased in some areas at the same time that walleye populations have declined. Researchers suggested that these fish could compete with or prey on walleye, particularly during their early life stages.Both McDermott Lake and Sandy Beach Lake had previously supported natural walleye recruitment. However, natural recruitment had last been detected in the two lakes in 2003–2004. Both lakes had also experienced declines in adult walleye numbers and were receiving stocked walleye fingerlings.To remove the centrarchid, researchers used fyke nets, mini-fyke nets, cloverleaf traps and boat electrofishing. The effort was extensive. Across the four years, the team used 107 hours of electrofishing, 717 fyke-net nights, 908 mini-fyke-net nights and 6,942 cloverleaf-trap nights.Bluegill accounted for the largest number of fish removed with 197,152 individuals. Largemouth bass followed with 35,168. Black crappie, green sunfish, pumpkinseed, rock bass and smallmouth bass were also removed.Black crappie relative abundance fell by about 83%, while rock bass declined by about 75%. Overall, the relative abundance of most centrarchid species fell by about 74% during the study.Yellow perch numbers surgeWhile the targeted fish declined, another species showed a striking increase. Yellow perch became much more abundant in McDermott Lake after the removals.Their catch per unit effort increased by about 788%, rising from roughly 8.9 fish per net to 79.11. Their average length also increased by about 18%, from 156 mm to 184 mm.The increase was much smaller in the reference lake. Yellow perch abundance there rose by about 116%, but the change was not statistically significant. Their average length in that lake fell slightly.Researchers said the response in McDermott Lake may have been linked to reduced competition or predation after the centrarchids were removed. However, they also noted that a particularly strong year class of yellow perch could have contributed to the increase.Yellow perch are also an important prey fish for walleye. Their abundance has been linked with walleye recruitment in other research. But despite the strong yellow perch response in McDermott Lake, the experiment did not produce detectable natural walleye recruitment.Walleye incresed, then fellAdult walleye numbers in McDermott Lake did show a temporary increase. After two years of fish removal, the estimated adult population reached about 120 in 2020.That increase did not continue. By 2021, the estimated adult walleye population had fallen to about 30–40, returning to levels seen before the removal programme.The researchers said the 2020 increase could not be linked to natural recruitment and stocked walleye from earlier years may have contributed to the temporary rise.Both lakes received extended-growth walleye fingerlings in 2017, 2019 and 2021. McDermott Lake received about 840 fish during each stocking, while Sandy Beach Lake received about 1,110. But no age-0 walleye were found during the study's recruitment surveys, because these surveys were conducted before the annual stocking, any age-0 walleye found would have been naturally produced.

articles.title: In 1921, a young Canadian doctor experimented with starving dogs; one dog's dramatic reaction helped lead to the discovery of insulin
articles.summary: Science News: In May 1921, Frederick Banting arrived at the University of Toronto with an idea about diabetes and little laboratory experience. Professor John J.R. .
articles.body: In May 1921, Frederick Banting arrived at the University of Toronto with an idea about diabetes and little laboratory experience. Professor John J.R. Macleod gave him space in the physiology department, several dogs and Charles Best, a young physiology student, as his assistant. They aimed to find the substance produced by the pancreas that appeared to regulate blood sugar. Banting and Best removed the pancreases of some dogs to produce diabetes artificially, while tying the pancreatic ducts of others so that the digestive part of the organ would deteriorate, leaving the insulin-producing islets behind. The work was difficult. Many of the animals died from complications and infection, and several of the duct-ligation operations failed. But on July 30, 1921, the researchers prepared their first pancreatic extract and injected it into a denervated dog known as Dog 410. Within an hour, its blood sugar had fallen from 0.20 per cent to 0.12 per cent, or about 200 to 120 milligrams per decilitre. Dog 410 died the following day, but the result gave Banting and Best their first clear evidence that they were on the right track.How a July 1921 experiment showed that a pancreatic extract could lower blood sugarThe July 30 experiment was not the discovery of a finished medicine. It was the first convincing result in a series of increasingly systematic experiments. Dog 410 had been made diabetic by removing its pancreas, and the extract injected into it had been prepared from the degenerated pancreas of another dog whose pancreatic duct had been tied off. The first injection produced the sharp fall in blood sugar that caught Banting and Best's attention, although subsequent injections that day produced less consistent results. The following morning, Dog 410 was found in a diabetic coma and died later that day. Two days later, another depancreatized dog, Dog 406, briefly improved after receiving the extract, with its blood sugar falling and the animal recovering enough to walk before it deteriorated again. Then came Dog 408, a yellow collie that received repeated injections of the extract from August 3 to 7. The experiments on these three dogs were imperfect, but together they convinced Banting and Best that the pancreatic extract had a real blood-sugar-lowering effect. They began referring to the substance as “isletin” in their laboratory notebooks.Why the dog named Marjorie became central to proving the extract could sustain lifeThe dog that later became the best-known animal in the insulin story was Marjorie, or Dog 33, but she was not the animal involved in the July breakthrough. Her pancreas was removed on November 18, 1921, months after the first experiments. She was subsequently kept alive with repeated doses of the evolving pancreatic extract. Unlike Dog 410, whose response was brief, Marjorie survived for 70 days after her pancreas was removed. The University of Toronto's scientific collections describe her survival as important evidence that the extract could sustain life in an animal without a functioning pancreas. By November, the researchers had also begun using pancreatic tissue from fetal calves, which offered a much more practical source of material than repeatedly preparing extracts from specially operated dogs. The work was moving from proof of principle toward finding a reliable way of producing enough active extract for further experiments. Marjorie's prolonged survival became one of the strongest demonstrations that the substance they were extracting could replace a function the body had lost.Why the famous rooftop photograph shows Dog 408, not MarjorieOne of the most persistent details in the popular story is also one of the easiest to get wrong. A famous photograph taken by Henry Mahon in August 1921 shows Banting and Best standing beside a dog on the roof of the University of Toronto's Medical Building. For years, the animal was identified as Marjorie. It was not. The University of Toronto archive identifies the dog as Dog 408, and the Nobel Prize's historical account makes the same correction. The dates alone expose the mistake: Marjorie did not enter the experiments until November, while Dog 408 was already being used in the pancreatic-extract trials in early August. Dog 408 received repeated injections of the extract and showed the blood-sugar-lowering effect that helped convince Banting and Best they had isolated something significant. The collie eventually died during the experiments, with an autopsy finding widespread infection. The photograph therefore captures the researchers during the early summer phase of the work, not the later period in which Marjorie became their longest-surviving test animal.How the dog experiments eventually led to insulin treatment in humansThe experiments on dogs established that a pancreatic extract could replace a missing function, but turning that crude extract into a treatment suitable for people required further work. James Collip, a biochemist who joined the group later in 1921, worked on improving the extraction and purification process. By January 1922, the team was ready to begin clinical testing. The first patient was 14-year-old Leonard Thompson, who received the refined extract at Toronto General Hospital on January 11, 1922, but the initial preparation produced little improvement and caused an abscess. After Collip further purified the extract, Thompson was treated again on January 23, with a dramatic improvement in his condition. Insulin rapidly moved from an experimental preparation to a treatment that could keep people with severe diabetes alive. Banting and Macleod were awarded the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin; Banting shared his prize money with Best, while Macleod shared his with Collip. The story therefore belongs to more than one researcher and more than one dog. Dog 410 provided the first striking blood-sugar result, Dog 408 became the animal in the famous photograph, and Marjorie demonstrated that the extract could sustain an animal for an extended period. Together, those experiments formed part of the chain that eventually turned insulin into a lifesaving treatment for humans.

articles.title: In 1995, Nasa sent 30 fertilised Japanese quail eggs to the Mir space station for 16 days; abnormalities developed in more than four times as many embryos as compared with the Earth ones
articles.summary: Science News: In 1995, a batch of fertilised Japanese quail eggs travelled from Earth to space station ‘Mir’ as part of an experiment designed to answer a question .
articles.body: In 1995, a batch of fertilised Japanese quail eggs travelled from Earth to space station ‘Mir’ as part of an experiment designed to answer a question that, ‘can embryos develop normally without the pull of gravity.’ 30 eggs were incubated aboard the station for 16 days before their developing embryos were preserved for examination on Earth. The results were striking. According to Nasa astronaut Shannon Lucid’s account of the mission, abnormalities appeared at more than four times the rate seen in the Earth-based control group. Later scientific records showed that many embryos developed broadly as expected, but some displayed problems affecting their eyes, limbs and beaks. The experiment offered a glimpse into the biological challenges of reproduction and development during long-term spaceflight far beyond Earth.Why did Nasa send fertilised Japanese quail eggs to the Mir space stationThe experiment was part of a wider effort to understand how living things respond to microgravity. As humans began considering longer stays in space, scientists also needed to understand whether the earliest stages of life could continue normally away from Earth. Nasa’s historical account of astronaut Shannon Lucid’s Mir mission explains that the quail experiment was among the first investigations she carried out after arriving on the space station. The fertilised Japanese quail eggs travelled to Mir on the same Space Shuttle flight that carried Lucid there and were placed in an onboard incubator.Over the following 16 days, Lucid removed the eggs individually and preserved the embryos for examination after their return to Earth. The task was more difficult than it might sound. The embryos had to be fixed in a chemical solution while floating in microgravity. According to Nasa’s, safety rules required several layers of containment because an escaped drop could float through the station and seriously injure a crew member. Engineers at Nasa’s Ames Research Center designed a specialised system of interlocking bags and attached gloves to allow the eggs to be handled safely. The unusual experiment was ultimately aimed at a much larger question: ‘how important is gravity during the earliest stages of life.’The embryos grew in an environment unlike anything on EarthOn Earth, bird eggs develop under the constant influence of gravity. Inside Mir, the eggs experienced microgravity while also being exposed to the other unusual conditions of spaceflight. The scientific record preserved by Nasa described experiments carried out during the 1995–1996 Mir programme. It found that most of the embryos examined after spaceflight had reached broadly expected stages of development. However, the results also revealed some differences. The space-grown embryos showed slight delays in growth when their body mass was compared with laboratory and synchronous control groups. Their body length followed a similar pattern. Some embryos also displayed visible abnormalities. Nasa specifically described problems involving the eyes, limbs and beaks. These included unusually small or defective eyes, twisted fingers and abnormalities affecting the beak. The findings showed that the space environment did not prevent embryonic growth altogether, but it could introduce risks that were not normally present under controlled conditions on Earth.What did the higher abnormality rate reveal about life in spaceIn her Nasa-published account of the mission, Shannon Lucid wrote that investigators found an abnormality rate of 13% among the embryos incubated on Mir. This was more than four times higher than the rate seen in the Earth-based control embryos. However, the results did not prove that microgravity alone was responsible. Lucid noted that investigators believed at least two other factors could have contributed to the higher rate of abnormalities. One was the slightly higher temperature inside the Mir incubator. The other was the considerably greater radiation exposure experienced aboard the space station. This made the experiment particularly important because space does not present just one changed condition. The absence of normal gravity exists alongside radiation exposure, differences in temperature and other environmental factors. Separating the influence of each factor remains a major challenge in space biology.A small experiment highlighted a much bigger challengeThe 30 Japanese quail eggs sent to Mir in 1995 represented a relatively small experiment, but the questions behind them were enormous. Nasa’s account of the mission showed the practical difficulties of carrying out delicate biological research in microgravity, while the later scientific records documented the results in greater detail. Most embryos reached broadly expected stages, but the higher abnormality rate and the growth differences showed that the space environment could not be treated as a simple substitute for conditions on Earth.The study was part of a broader series of investigations into avian embryogenesis during the joint Mir/Space Shuttle and Mir/Nasa science programmes. Researchers were examining how the earliest stages of life responded when the environmental conditions familiar on Earth were dramatically altered. The quail experiment therefore contributed to a growing area of research with implications for longer missions. As space agencies considered journeys lasting months or even years, understanding how living systems respond to space became increasingly important. Mir helped expose some of the biggest questions about the future of life beyond Earth.

articles.title: What it's like to ride in Uber's new self-driving taxis in London
articles.summary: The ride-hailing app has launched 15 self-driving taxis, but they will have safety drivers inside.
articles.body:
Londoners are able to hail the UK's first robotaxis - as Uber today becomes the first company to launch a self-driving minicab.

Initially, it only has 15 autonomous vehicles with a licence to operate in the city, and each one must have a human safety driver behind the wheel ready to take control if anything goes wrong.

Uber said it surveyed London-based customers via the app and more than 100,000 said they would choose a self-driving taxi if one was available, despite incidents of driverless rides malfunctioning in US cities where they already operate.

As I found out when I became the first UK journalist to hail one, it was mostly smooth but the safety driver did intervene on one occasion.

At the moment the UK fare for a robotaxi ride will be the same fare as a standard UberX, Uber Electric, or Uber Comfort journey, with upfront fares shown in the app.

Taking a self-driving ride will only appear as an option in the app after the journey has been booked, and if one of its cars is available nearby.

Uber's global head of autonomous mobility and delivery Sarfraz Maredia said the plan was to phase them in over a period of several years.

"We always want consumers to be able to request a human ride or an autonomous vehicle, and because the market's growing, we expect that there will be human drivers on Uber London for a long time to come," he said.

The Ford Mustang electric vehicles which make up Uber's current small fleet are fitted with the UK tech firm Wayve's driverless car technology, which uses AI to analyse data about what is going on around it in real time, gathered by sensors in a bar on the roof of the vehicle and elsewhere.

The vehicles are not pre-programmed - their actions are determined on the spot depending on what is going on.

Google's autonomous car company Waymo and the Chinese tech giant Baidu are also vying to launch services in the UK, and the competition is fierce.

Wayve chief executive Alex Kendall described developing the technology as "the space race for our generation" but added there were some "really hard problems to solve" along the way.

"What we've done over time is pioneer a completely new approach to autonomous driving, making it possible to bring this to a busy and complex city like London and scale it globally," he said.

'The driver took the wheel' - what was it like to ride in?

This week I became the first British journalist to travel as a customer in a self-driving Uber after hailing one via the app.

The safety driver gave me a 30-second safety briefing, and then we were off, making our way down the busy streets of central London.

For several minutes, we negotiated the traffic without incident, cruising past a busy Brexit demonstration underway outside parliament, successfully navigating traffic lights and roadworks along the way.

When a cyclist paused and waved us forward at a mini roundabout with his arm, the car complied.

But at one point the safety driver did have to take control of the car.

Just as we were pulling off, the back doors of a van parked beside us on a narrow side road appeared to swing open. The car braked sharply, an internal alarm beeped, and the driver took the wheel.

Wayve later told me it was the driver's decision to intervene and they were confident their AI system would have handled it.

The drama was all over in a couple of seconds - but it was perhaps the perfect illustration that while the industry may be in a rush, the UK's regulators are not.

Earlier this year, the government and the industry had suggested that there could be fully driverless cars for hire in London by the end of 2026, but this is looking increasingly unlikely.

The Department for Transport (DfT) and the regional authority Transport for London (TfL) are responsible for overseeing the process and have faced criticism for being slow.

A DfT spokesperson said the government department was working towards a framework being put in place to ensure self-driving cars could be on the roads in 2027, but didn't give a specific date.

"These services will be introduced carefully, subject to rigorous safety testing and regulatory approval and will require local consent which can consider the potential impacts on local roads, jobs and communities," the department said in a statement.

Christina Calderator, director of transport strategy and policy at TfL, said they were "not holding up any decision" on the cars, but instead "taking time to get it right".

"This is something that's new, it's coming to London - we need to make sure it's safe," she said.

David McMullen, senior organiser for the trade union GMB, said caution needed to be taken with the roll-out of driverless cars unless people were "prepared to see unprecedented levels of social and economic disruption".

He called on TfL and the government to develop a plan that "protects drivers" and said until one was put in place, it was "premature" to move to driverless services.

Waymo - another driverless car firm owned by Google's Alphabet - has cars which have been driving London's streets for several months carrying out mapping.

These cars currently have a safety driver and members of staff in them - but are not yet for the public.

The firm says it does not intend to introduce a service that would include a human at the wheel.

Experts said there were still numerous safety challenges around self-driving cars for regulators to consider.

Prof Siddartha Khastgir, head of safe autonomy at the University of Warwick's Warwick Manufacturing Group said there were numerous safety challenges for regulators to consider.

"As human drivers we tend to make a very conscious decision of what we believe is right, and sometimes actually do things that are not perfectly legal - so for example, we tend to mount the kerb to give way to an ambulance," he said.

"So, how does a self-driving vehicle respond to emergency services? And what are the nuances of doing that in a crowded place like London?"

articles.title: A fungus turns beetles into zombies and makes them die on flowers; scientists say the timing helps infect the next generation
articles.summary: Science News: A fungus infecting goldenrod soldier beetles can alter their behaviour before death and cause changes to their bodies afterwards. Researchers investig.
articles.body: A fungus infecting goldenrod soldier beetles can alter their behaviour before death and cause changes to their bodies afterwards. Researchers investigating Eryniopsis lampyridarum found infected Chauliognathus pensylvanicus beetles clamped their mandibles tightly onto flower heads shortly before dying. Between 15 and 22 hours after death, the fungus caused the beetles to raise their hardened forewings and expand their hind wings, with these changes occurring mainly between midnight and 7 am. The researchers recorded infected beetles on frost aster, common boneset and Canada goldenrod during investigations in Arkansas. In one 1996 collection of 446 beetles, 90 were infected, producing an overall prevalence of 20.2%. The study found that infected beetles developed either conidia or resting spores, but not both. The researchers said the positioning of infected beetles on flowers may increase opportunities for fungal spores to reach other hosts, although the mechanism behind the pre-death gripping behaviour remains unknown.How does the fungus turn beetles into zombiesAccording to the study published ScienceDirect titled ‘Zombie soldier beetles: Epizootics in the goldenrod soldier beetle, Chauliognathus pensylvanicus (Coleoptera: Cantharidae) caused by Eryniopsis lampyridarum (Entomophthoromycotina: Entomophthoraceae)’, infected beetles displayed a striking behaviour shortly before death. They tightly clamped their mandibles into flower heads, firmly attaching themselves to plants. Such behaviour, also seen in other fungal infections, may help fungal spores reach new hosts. Goldenrod soldier beetles normally feed on pollen from Asteraceae plants and gather on flowers for mating.Researchers found infected beetles attached to frost aster, common boneset and Canada goldenrod. At the University of Arkansas Experiment Station, large numbers of dead beetles were found attached to frost aster flowers on 3 October 1996, with fungal structures covering their abdomens. Similar outbreaks occurred in Washington County, Arkansas, between 25 September and 19 October in four different years.Why do zombie beetles raise their wings after deathThe fungal effects continued after the beetles had died. Researchers observed the insects periodically for 24 hours after death and recorded changes in their bodies. About 15 to 22 hours after the beetles died, usually between midnight and 7 am, the fungus caused the dead insects to raise their elytra, the hardened forewings found in beetles, and expand their metathoracic wings. These changes occurred after death rather than before it. The researchers specifically noted that the mechanism responsible for the beetles' flowers before death remained unknown.The position of the dead beetles on flowers is relevant to fungal transmission because the fungus produces spores from the infected host. The study's introduction explains that some fungal pathogens alter host behaviour so infected insects remain in locations where spores have a greater chance of contacting other hosts. In E. lampyridarum, the beetles died while firmly attached to flower heads, with their bodies positioned on the plants where the fungus could develop and produce its reproductive structures. The researchers described the study as providing the first detailed information on the plants associated with infected beetles and the first detailed observations of the fungus's resting spores.Why does the fungus appear in autumnInfections mainly occur during the autumn, when adult goldenrod soldier beetles are present on flowering plants. The researchers reported fungal outbreaks in Arkansas between late September and October across several study years. Because the beetles are univoltine, meaning they have one generation each year, the timing of infection occurs during the adult stage of their annual life cycle. Adults feed on pollen-producing plants, while their larval stages have been reported to prey on ticks and on eggs and larvae of tiger beetles.The researchers did not establish a direct mechanism showing that the fungus specifically infects the next beetle generation. However, they documented several features relevant to transmission: infected adults attach to flowers before death, fungal structures develop on the dead insects, and outbreaks occur in the autumn period when adult beetles are found on flowering plants. The study concluded that the interaction provides information on fungal prevalence, beetle-plant associations and the effects of the fungus on its host. It also recorded the production of both conidia and resting spores, providing evidence of different fungal stages within infected beetles.

articles.title: Heathrow expansion 'a risk we cannot afford to take', says mayor
articles.summary: Sir Sadiq Khan is repeating his opposition to a third runway in response to a government consultation.
articles.body:
The London mayor has formally opposed plans for a third runway at Heathrow Airport, arguing the expansion threatens environmental targets and transport networks.

City Hall and Transport for London (TfL) submitted a joint response to the government's draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement (HENPS) consultation.

Sir Sadiq Khan claimed the strategic case relied on outdated evidence that "fails to reflect current climate laws and travel habits".

The government said it was reviewing the response, while Heathrow questioned many of the claims made in City Hall's submission.

The airport said the expansion was the "most important economic growth opportunity available to the UK".

But Sir Sadiq said he saw no evidence the proposals were compatible with a credible path to net zero.

"The evidence suggests Heathrow expansion is a risk that we simply cannot afford to take."

City Hall said additional flights could reverse the progress in reducing air pollution in communities surrounding Heathrow brought by the Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez).

The submission raised several issues regarding infrastructure and finance:

TfL estimates targets in the draft policy could generate 60,000 additional daily highway trips, adding 22 million road journeys annually to the M4 and M25

Capacity upgrades would be needed for the Elizabeth and Piccadilly lines, alongside new southern and western rail links. TfL put the potential surface access cost at £9bn, noting no funding agreement exists

TfL said a 58% increase in flights would reduce predictable noise respite periods for local residents from 50% to 25% of the day

"The whole case for Heathrow expansion relies on outdated evidence that fails to take into account the urgent challenges we face today," Sir Sadiq said.

"I will continue to vehemently oppose these plans as I seek to build a fairer, safer, greener, more prosperous London for everyone."

Heathrow Airport Limited is preparing plans for a new 2.1 mile (3.5km) northwest runway - which would require realigning a section of the M25 - with a final decision expected following a parliamentary vote in 2029.

A spokesperson for the airport rejected claims that expansion was incompatible with net zero goals - and said the airport was committed to a completely privately-funded noise insulation scheme for local homes.

On transport infrastructure, Heathrow stated its expansion plans include widening a busy stretch of the M25, adding that it will present "viable and funded solutions" for required public transport upgrades as part of the planning process.

"This is about much more than a new runway.

"It's about unlocking growth and over 100,000 jobs for the whole country, boosting British trade by £150bn, making travel more affordable and revitalising the UK's steel industry."

The mayor's stance is backed by a coalition of London and home counties council leaders - including Wandsworth, Richmond, Kingston, Hillingdon, Southwark, Sutton, and Windsor and Maidenhead.

In a joint letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander following the consultation's close, the cross-party group called on the government to withdraw support for the third runway.

However, the Back Heathrow campaign pushed back against the councils, claiming their opposition was "not representative" of local residents.

Executive director Parmjit Dhanda said more than 100,000 local members support the expansion, citing the potential for jobs, trade, and economic growth, adding that a new runway was "way overdue".

The Department for Transport, which threw its support behind expansion under Keir Starmer's premiership in 2025, said ministers would "carefully consider all responses before setting out next steps later this year".

"We have always been clear that expansion will only go ahead if it is delivered in line with our legally binding climate change obligations, and meets strict environmental rules on air quality and noise pollution," a spokesperson for the department added.

Analysis: Tom Edwards, BBC London transport correspondent

The position of the mayor and TfL against expansion at Heathrow hasn't changed -they have always had concerns over noise pollution, public transport and extra traffic.

What is different this time is they think the modelling is outdated, and the language seems to have toughened.

Perhaps Ulez has empowered the mayor to be more direct?

TfL said since the pandemic, the world had changed with a decline in business travel. They also said the figures being used to back expansion are over ten years old and no longer relevant.

It leaves the mayor potentially on a collision course with the pro-expansion lobby - including those within his own party.

articles.title: En 1994, investigadores tiraron neumáticos desechados a un canal: se convirtieron en arrecifes submarinos con 20 veces más peces a su alrededor
articles.standfirst: Un experimento que invita a replantear algunas estrategias bajo el agua
articles.summary: Un experimento que invita a replantear algunas estrategias bajo el agua
articles.body: Hace más de 30 años, un grupo de investigadores de California y Arizona decidieron probar suerte con una especie de experimento que, a día de hoy, ha resultado ser todo un éxito que ha devuelto la vida a un entorno que en 1994 era complejo. Algo tan increíble como lanzar neumáticos desechados a un canal ha derivado en arrecifes submarinos con 20 veces más peces. Gordon Mueller y Charles R. Liston, en la década de los 90, respondieron a los intentos de ingenieros por solucionar un problema, ya que al recubrir con hormigón los canales del suroeste de Estados Unidos, impidieron que el agua se filtrase al suelo y la vegetación creciese, provocando que la presencia de peces disminuyera. Estos investigadores optaron por una solución un tanto desesperada tanto en el Canal de Coachella como en el Acueducto Hayden-Rhodes: colocar neumáticos desechados en el agua, en una especie de arrecife donde, contra todo pronóstico, se asentaron algas, insectos y organismos que comenzaron a alimentar y dar cobijo a los peces. Después de un tiempo, la cantidad de peces era 20 veces mayor que antes y, además, la presencia de invertebrados era tres veces mayor. Esto había sido provocado por el simple gesto de dejar esos neumáticos y crear esos arrecifes, dando una nueva vida al entorno acuático de la región. El comportamiento de los peces cambió por completo, ya que sin los neumáticos, toda la superficie y estructura sería lisa, por lo que un cambio en su entorno les dio la oportunidad de crear nuevas posibilidades, refugio, alimento y un entorno mucho más estable. Así, lo que parecía destinado a ser un desecho, acabó siendo crucial para dar vida a un canal casi desaparecido que los peces prácticamente habían abandonado.

articles.title: Your AI may soon be able to pay for things through UPI without asking every single time: Here is how India plans to control it
articles.summary: Science News: India’s digital payment journey has evolved from passwords, PINs and OTPs to fingerprints and facial authentication, making transactions faster and mo.
articles.body: India’s digital payment journey has evolved from passwords, PINs and OTPs to fingerprints and facial authentication, making transactions faster and more seamless. Now, with AI, the next step could be completely hands-free payments, where systems recognise users, assess transactions and authenticate payments almost invisibly.The country may allow AI agents to make small UPI payments without asking the owner every single time, as per a report by Reuters. The proposed framework called the Unified Agent Protocol could be unveiled at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai next week, said the sources to the agency.While the proposal has not been formally confirmed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NCPI), if introduced in the reported form, it would allow users to give AI agents limited authority to make payments based on pre-set instructions rather than approving each transaction individually.What could possibly changeInitially, the use cases are expected to focus on small and frequent payments, such as grocery purchases, as per the agency. E-commerce platforms could be among the early areas where such payments are used. Over time, potential use cases could extend to more complex transactions.Reuters reported that AI agents could potentially identify offers and discounts and place orders based on user-defined instructions. Further advanced applications could include investments based on specific price thresholds, though such uses would depend on the way the framework is ultimately designed and regulated.The reported system could use existing UPI mechanisms such as UPI Circle, which allows payment authority to be delegated and Reserve Pay, which enables funds to be set aside for specified payments. According to the Reuters report, NPCI is also expected to provide infrastructure allowing merchants to integrate with the system. Users could potentially set rules covering how much an AI agent can spend and when it can make a payment.Spending limits, identity checks and audit trails are the safeguards being considered reportedly. The agency also reported that NPCI plans to establish a liability framework, although details were not available.This would mean that AI would not have complete authority in initiating a payment. The proposed model would allow a user to give the agent pre-authorised, rule-based payment authority, within the limited set by the system.What other countries and payment networks are doingIndia is not the only country developing agentic payments. Payment networks and fintech companies in other markets are also working in the same direction to allow AI agents to participate in commerce. Mastercard has developed Agent Pay, an infrastructure designed to allow AI agents to conduct payments while using controls around trust, security and transaction visibility.Visa has also been developing infrastructure for agent-led commerce. The broader approach being explored by payment companies is to allow an AI agent to search for products, make choices based on instructions and initiate transactions, while retaining authentication and other controls.In India, Mastercard has already conducted agentic commerce transactions with businesses, while fintech companies including Pine Labs have also been developing infrastructure for AI-led payments.As of now, the reported framework is still a proposed development. Its final features, transaction limits, safeguards, liability rules and rollout timeline would depend on what NPCI formally announces.

articles.title: Scientists rediscover a ‘ghost’ green mamba hidden in a Polish museum for decades after its 1885 discovery
articles.summary: Science News: A green mamba specimen from São Tomé Island that dates back to 1885 has been found after decades of being regarded as lost, which gives scientists a r.
articles.body: A green mamba specimen from São Tomé Island that dates back to 1885 has been found after decades of being regarded as lost, which gives scientists a rare opportunity to revisit the identity of one of the Gulf of Guinea’s most mysterious snakes. Adolfo Möller found the specimen during an expedition to the island, after which zoologist Jacques Vladimir von Bedriaga examined it. According to the study published in Bio One Digital Library titled ‘The materialization of a ghost: redescription of Bedriaga’s ‘lost’ specimen of Green Mamba (Elapidae: Dendroaspis) from São Tomé Island’, researchers eventually found the specimen in the collections of the Museum and Institute of Zoology of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Warsaw. Its significance became even clearer because other historical specimens from São Tomé had disappeared, which leaves fewer clues to resolve the snake’s identity. The preserved mamba now allows scientists to examine its physical features and revisit more than a century of conflicting classifications.The ‘ghost’ green mamba was hiding in a Polish museum for decadesThe snake was found by Adolfo Frederico Möller between May and September 1885 during an expedition to São Tomé. Möller was primarily a botanist, but he also gathered zoological specimens during his work on the island. According to the study, the green mamba was later examined by Jacques Vladimir von Bedriaga, who described the specimen in the early 1890s. Two other historical green mamba specimens from São Tomé were also lost during the Second World War, leaving researchers with little surviving material to investigate the identity of the island’s mysterious snake. That changed when scientists reviewed natural history collections containing specimens from São Tomé and Príncipe and came across Bedriaga’s mamba in Warsaw. The specimen was preserved under catalogue number MIZ 73634 and had remained in the collection despite being considered lost.Why the identity of São Tomé’s mysterious green mamba remained a mysteryThe identity of the São Tomé green mamba has remained difficult to establish because there was very little historical material available. Bedriaga originally identified his specimen as Dendroaspis angusticeps, the eastern green mamba. Portuguese zoologist José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage later assigned it a different identity, while Johann Georg Fischer had earlier placed another São Tomé specimen in a proposed new genus. The rediscovery of Bedriaga’s specimen has now changed that. Scientists were able to examine its scales, measurements and other external features and compare them with recognised Dendroaspis species. The specimen showed considerable morphological similarity to the western green mamba, Dendroaspis viridis.What the rediscovered specimen revealed about the mysterious snakeThe re-examination also helped explain several unusual features noted in earlier descriptions. Bedriaga had recorded an unusually low number of subcaudal scales and described what appeared to be a scale covering the tip of the tail. The specimen also showed signs of an injury near the abdomen, which researchers said was consistent with the snake that was being shot from a tree before it was preserved. Its scale counts and body proportions were within the ranges documented for Dendroaspis viridis. These physical characteristics strengthen the connection with the western green mamba while also helping explain some of the unusual details in the earlier descriptions.The rediscovered specimen may answer one question about São Tomé’s mysterious green mamba, but it raises another: could the snake still survive on the island? The study does not establish that a living population remains there, and recent searches have not produced fresh specimens. The researchers note that an arboreal snake can be difficult to detect in forested habitats, leaving its present status uncertain.

articles.title: Meet the 'Turtle Women' of Amazon: 7 Indigenous women are bringing vulnerable river turtles back from the brink after releasing 208 baby turtles into the wild
articles.summary: Science News: Seven Indigenous Siekopai women in Ecuador’s Amazon are using ancestral knowledge, modern technology and community-led conservation to give vulnerable.
articles.body: Seven Indigenous Siekopai women in Ecuador’s Amazon are using ancestral knowledge, modern technology and community-led conservation to give vulnerable river turtles a better chance of survival. Known as the Tari Nomiowa’i, or “Turtle Women”, the group patrols the banks of the Aguarico River in search of charapa turtle nests, carefully collects eggs threatened by flooding, predators and human activity, and raises the hatchlings in protected conditions before returning them to the river. During the 2025-26 nesting season, the women collected 235 eggs and successfully hatched and released 208 young turtles into the Aguarico River in March and April 2026. Their work is not only helping protect Podocnemis unifilis, also known as the yellow-spotted Amazon River turtle, but is also preserving an Indigenous relationship with the river and its wildlife.How seven Indigenous women became the ‘Turtle Women’ of the AmazonThe conservation effort is centred on seven Siekopai women who call themselves Tari Nomiowa’i, a name that translates as “Turtle Women”. Their work combines traditional ecological knowledge passed down through generations with modern conservation techniques. Janeth Piaguaje, a Siekopai community leader involved in the project, learned how to handle turtle eggs from her father, including how to recognise nesting periods and identify suitable nests along the riverbanks. The women now patrol the Aguarico River looking for tracks and nests and record information including the date, time, location and number of eggs using the Epicollect5 field-data collection app.Their approach allows knowledge that has traditionally been passed between generations to be combined with systematic records that can help conservationists understand nesting patterns and measure the results of their work. Rather than separating conservation from Indigenous life, the project places local women and their knowledge at the centre of efforts to protect a species that has long been part of the community's relationship with the river.Why the Amazon river turtles are under growing pressureThe charapa turtle faces several threats across its range, with human activity placing particular pressure on populations. Adult turtles are hunted for meat, while their eggs can be collected from nests for consumption. Pollution is another problem, with rubbish, plastic and discarded materials entering waterways and nesting areas. Along the Aguarico River, the women have also observed dead animals floating downstream and regularly encounter plastic and garbage on the beaches where turtles nest. Boat traffic can contribute to erosion of riverbanks, while changing water levels associated with climate change can flood the low-lying areas where turtles lay their eggs.The combination of these pressures can make natural reproduction difficult because eggs and nests are exposed to threats before hatchlings ever reach the water. The species is classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, meaning it faces a high risk of extinction in the wild in the medium term if the threats affecting it are not adequately addressed. Protecting nesting sites is therefore an important part of giving the species a better chance of maintaining and rebuilding populations.How the women rescue eggs and raise baby turtlesWhen the Turtle Women find nests at risk, they carefully collect the eggs and transport them to an incubation facility where they can develop under controlled and protected conditions. The eggs are kept away from predators, pollution and flooding that could destroy nests in the wild. The women monitor the eggs until they hatch and then continue caring for the young turtles for about another month before releasing them. During this period, the hatchlings are fed locally available plant foods including cassava, sweet potato and taro leaves. The process effectively gives the young turtles a protected start to life during one of their most vulnerable stages.The women also document their work digitally, recording information about individual nests and the number of eggs collected. This creates a record of the project's performance and provides information that can be used when planning future conservation activities. Such intervention does not remove all the dangers facing the turtles once they return to the river, but it can substantially reduce the immediate risks of nest flooding, predation and human disturbance during the egg and early hatchling stages.208 hatchlings returned to the Aguarico RiverThe 2025-26 nesting season provided a significant result for the community-led project. The seven women collected 235 eggs and successfully hatched 208 young turtles, which were released into the Aguarico River during March and April 2026. The releases became more than a conservation exercise because the women invited members of the local community, including schoolchildren, to take part and attend educational workshops. These activities gave younger generations an opportunity to see the turtles being returned to their natural environment and learn why their nests and habitats need protection. One child reportedly told Piaguaje that she would look after the turtles and tell others not to touch their eggs, illustrating how the project is also trying to change attitudes towards wildlife.The 208 releases represent a strong short-term outcome for the programme, but they should not be interpreted as proof that the wider wild population has already recovered. The turtles will still face predators, pollution, habitat pressures and other dangers after release, making continued protection of the river and nesting beaches essential to turning successful hatchling production into lasting population recovery.Protecting turtles also means protecting Siekopai cultureFor the Turtle Women, the project has significance that goes beyond wildlife management. The Siekopai have an ancestral relationship with the river and its animals, and the women see the turtles as part of a cultural and spiritual connection with nature. According to Piaguaje, the turtles are linked to the visible and spiritual worlds and are protected by Koouwajëo, regarded in their tradition as the spiritual chief, mother and ancestral guardian of the turtles. This belief provides an important cultural motivation for the conservation work.Protecting the turtles is therefore understood not simply as saving an animal but as honouring the river, maintaining cultural traditions and passing knowledge to younger generations. The project also demonstrates how Indigenous communities can combine traditional ecological knowledge with tools such as digital mapping and nest monitoring to address modern conservation challenges. The seven women are now part of a wider effort to ensure that the Aguarico River continues to support both wildlife and the communities whose lives and traditions are closely connected to it. Their work shows that conservation can become more effective and meaningful when local communities are not simply participants in wildlife projects but are the people leading them.

articles.title: In 2003, crews began removing non-native fish from the Grand Canyon; by 2006 rainbow trout’s share of the catch had fallen from about 90% to under 10%
articles.summary: Science News: In the depths of the Grand Canyon, scientists were trying to give native fish a better chance of survival, by taking other fish out of the Colorado Ri.
articles.body: In the depths of the Grand Canyon, scientists were trying to give native fish a better chance of survival, by taking other fish out of the Colorado River. A four-year fish-removal experiment conducted between 2003 and 2006 dramatically changed the composition of fish being caught in one section of the river. According to a 2011 study by Michael D. Coggins Jr., Michael D. Yard and William E. Pine III, published in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society and available through the U.S. Geological Survey, rainbow trout went from making up about 90% of the catch at the beginning of the experiment to less than 10% by August 2006. But the story was more complicated than simply removing an invasive species and watching native fish return.Why were the fish being removed?The target was the federally protected humpback chub, a native fish of the Colorado River that had faced major ecological pressures. The humpback chub is specially adapted to the warm, sediment-rich and fast-flowing waters that historically characterized the river. After the construction of Glen Canyon Dam, the river’s conditions changed substantially, including becoming colder and clearer in many areas. Those changes helped create conditions in which introduced trout could thrive.Rainbow and brown trout can prey on native fish, including humpback chub, while also competing with them for resources. The National Park Service identifies invasive fish as one of the continuing challenges facing native fish populations in the Grand Canyon. So researchers set out to test whether reducing the number of non-native fish could improve conditions for native species.More than 36,500 fish were caughtDuring the 2003–2006 experiment, crews captured more than 36,500 fish belonging to 15 species in the mechanical-removal reach. About 64% of the total catch was made up of non-native fish. Rainbow trout alone accounted for 19,020 fish, followed by fathead minnows, common carp and brown trout.Native fish made up the remaining 36%, including more than 7,300 flannelmouth suckers, 2,600 humpback chub, 2,200 bluehead suckers and more than 1,000 speckled dace. The change in the catch was striking. Rainbow trout’s contribution fell steadily from approximately 90% in January 2003 to below 10% in August 2006. The overall share of non-native fish also fell sharply, from more than 95% at the beginning of the experiment to below 50% after July 2005.Native fish appeared to benefit but scientists couldn’t take all the creditThe researchers also observed an increase in juvenile native fish within the removal area, suggesting that reducing non-native fish may have improved native fish survival and recruitment. Yet the scientists were careful about claiming a straightforward cause-and-effect victory.During the same period, drought increased river temperatures, while rainbow trout abundance was declining across the wider river system. Those simultaneous changes made it difficult to determine exactly how much of the improvement in native fish recruitment came from the removal program itself and how much resulted from changing environmental conditions. That uncertainty is reflected in the study’s title: Nonnative fish control in the Colorado River in Grand Canyon, Arizona: An effective program or serendipitous timing?The battle did not end in 2006The experiment became part of a much larger effort to protect the Grand Canyon’s native fish. Today, the National Park Service continues to control invasive trout in parts of the Colorado River system, including through electrofishing and trapping. Its conservation work also includes moving humpback chub into suitable tributaries and monitoring native fish populations.The humpback chub itself has since been downlisted from endangered to threatened status, but it remains a conservation priority. Grand Canyon National Park contains the largest remaining population of the species. The 2003–2006 experiment therefore offers a revealing lesson in conservation: removing a non-native predator can rapidly reshape an ecosystem, but nature rarely provides a single explanation for what happens next. In the Grand Canyon, the falling numbers of rainbow trout coincided with other environmental changes, leaving scientists to disentangle how much was deliberate intervention and how much was timing.
